title: How do you implement CDC (Change Data Capture) in Databricks — using `MERGE INTO` on Delta tables for batch CDC, or DLT's `APPLY CHANGES INTO` for streaming CDC from Debezium/Kafka change feeds?
shortTitle: How do you implement CDC (Change Data Capture) in Databricks

s1_definition.profdef: Change Data Capture is the practice of capturing inserts, updates, and deletes that happen in a source system and applying those same changes to a target table so the target stays in sync. In Databricks you implement it two main ways: for batch CDC you use `MERGE INTO` on a Delta table to atomically match incoming change records against existing rows and insert, update, or delete accordingly, and for streaming CDC you use Delta Live Tables' `APPLY CHANGES INTO`, which consumes an ordered change feed from a tool like Debezium through Kafka and handles the upsert and delete logic, out-of-order events, and sequencing for you.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a master customer ledger, and throughout the day a source system records every change: a new customer opened an account, an address was updated, a closed account was deleted. Change Data Capture is the process of taking that running list of changes and faithfully applying each one to the master ledger so it always matches reality. With `MERGE INTO` you are a careful clerk who, in one atomic pass, looks at each change and decides: this is a new customer so add a page, this is an update so overwrite the existing page, this is a deletion so remove the page. With `APPLY CHANGES INTO` you hand that whole job to an automated assistant that continuously watches the live change feed and keeps the ledger in sync, even sorting out changes that arrive slightly out of order.
s1_definition.oneliner: In Databricks, CDC keeps a target in sync with a source's inserts, updates, and deletes, using Delta `MERGE INTO` for batch upserts and Delta Live Tables `APPLY CHANGES INTO` for streaming change feeds from Debezium or Kafka.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Change Data Capture is the practice of capturing inserts, updates, and deletes that happen in a source system and applying those same changes to a target table so the target stays in sync. In Databricks you implement it two main ways: for batch CDC you use `MERGE INTO` on a Delta table to atomically match incoming change records against existing rows and insert, update, or delete accordingly, and for streaming CDC you use Delta Live Tables' `APPLY CHANGES INTO`, which consumes an ordered change feed from a tool like Debezium through Kafka and handles the upsert and delete logic, out-of-order events, and sequencing for you.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a master customer ledger, and throughout the day a source system records every change: a new customer opened an account, an address was updated, a closed account was deleted. Change Data Capture is the process of taking that running list of changes and faithfully applying each one to the master ledger so it always matches reality. With `MERGE INTO` you are a careful clerk who, in one atomic pass, looks at each change and decides: this is a new customer so add a page, this is an update so overwrite the existing page, this is a deletion so remove the page. With `APPLY CHANGES INTO` you hand that whole job to an automated assistant that continuously watches the live change feed and keeps the ledger in sync, even sorting out changes that arrive slightly out of order.

**One line to remember:** In Databricks, CDC keeps a target in sync with a source's inserts, updates, and deletes, using Delta `MERGE INTO` for batch upserts and Delta Live Tables `APPLY CHANGES INTO` for streaming change feeds from Debezium or Kafka.

sections.s2_technical:
Change Data Capture matters because you rarely want to reload an entire source table every time something changes; you want to apply only the deltas. The source emits change records, each typically carrying the operation type, insert, update, or delete, the row's key, the new values, and a sequence or timestamp indicating order. Your job is to apply these to a target Delta table so it mirrors the source.

For batch CDC, the core tool is Delta Lake's `MERGE INTO`. You merge a batch of change records against the target on the primary key, and in one atomic transaction you specify what to do in each case. A typical statement reads merge into the target using the changes on the key, when matched and the operation is delete then delete, when matched then update all the columns, and when not matched then insert. This gives you an atomic upsert-and-delete, and because Delta is ACID the whole merge either fully applies or not at all, with concurrent readers always seeing a consistent snapshot. A subtlety is handling multiple changes to the same key in one batch: you must first reduce to the latest change per key using the sequence column, often with a window function picking the row with the highest sequence, otherwise the merge is ambiguous. You run this merge on each micro-batch or each scheduled batch of captured changes.

For streaming CDC, Delta Live Tables provides `APPLY CHANGES INTO`, which is purpose-built for continuous change feeds. You typically capture changes at the database with Debezium, which reads the database transaction log and publishes change events to Kafka, and Auto Loader or a Kafka source brings them into a bronze table. Then `APPLY CHANGES INTO` a target table, specifying the key columns, the sequence column that defines ordering, and optionally columns to ignore, and it handles the upsert and delete semantics, including out-of-order events, by using the sequence to apply only the latest change per key. It also supports deletes via a configured delete condition and can produce slowly changing dimension type one, which overwrites, or type two, which keeps history with effective and end dates. This removes the hand-written merge, deduplication, and ordering logic you would otherwise maintain.

A senior-level nuance is Delta's own Change Data Feed feature, enabled with a table property, which makes a Delta table emit its own row-level changes that downstream consumers can read incrementally, so Delta tables can be both the target of CDC and a source of CDC for further layers. Another nuance is ordering and idempotency: CDC is only correct if you apply changes in the right order per key and the operation is idempotent so replays after a failure do not corrupt the target, which is exactly why the sequence column and the atomicity of merge matter. The practical rule at a bank is to use merge for batch or micro-batch CDC where you control the batching, and apply-changes-into for continuous streaming CDC from a log-based capture tool, always reducing to the latest change per key and relying on Delta's ACID guarantees so a mid-stream failure leaves the target consistent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the core banking database holds the authoritative account records, and the analytics lakehouse needs a copy that stays current. Reloading the whole accounts table every hour was wasteful and slow. Instead the source emits change records for each insert, update, and delete. This is exactly the CDC problem: apply only the deltas to keep the lakehouse accounts table in sync.

This is exactly how CDC in Databricks works. For a batch of captured changes you use merge into to atomically insert new accounts, update changed ones, and delete closed ones against the Delta accounts table on the account id key.

Problem 2 — Sometimes a batch contains two changes for the same account, like an address update followed by a balance update, and the events can arrive slightly out of order. If you merge naively you might apply the older change last and lose the newer value. The fix is to reduce to the latest change per key using the sequence number before merging, which is also exactly what apply changes into does automatically for streaming feeds.

Because we cannot run real Delta merges here, this runnable demo models CDC faithfully. A `DeltaTable` holds rows keyed by account id and supports an atomic merge. A `ChangeRecord` carries the operation, key, values, and a sequence. A `BatchCdcMerger` reduces to the latest change per key and applies insert, update, delete in one pass. A `StreamingCdcApplier` models apply changes into by consuming an ordered feed and applying only the latest sequence per key, including deletes. The demo applies a batch of changes with duplicates and out-of-order sequences to show correct upsert and delete, then streams a feed to show the apply-changes behavior.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
cdc:
  key-columns: [account_id]
  sequence-column: seq
  apply-as-deletes: "op = 'DELETE'"
  scd-type: 1              # 1 = overwrite, 2 = keep history
source:
  debezium-topic: dbserver.bank.accounts
```

Java source files:
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/databricks-cdc-sim-1.0.0.jar com.bank.cdc.CdcDemo

# Real Databricks batch CDC (SQL):
# MERGE INTO accounts t USING latest_changes s ON t.account_id = s.account_id
# WHEN MATCHED AND s.op='DELETE' THEN DELETE
# WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
# WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op!='DELETE' THEN INSERT *;
#
# Real DLT streaming CDC (Python):
# dlt.apply_changes(target="accounts", source="bronze_cdc",
#   keys=["account_id"], sequence_by="seq", apply_as_deletes="op = 'DELETE'",
#   stored_as_scd_type=1)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Delta accounts table seeded with Rajesh and Priya, a batch of change records including a new account, two out-of-order updates to Rajesh, and a delete of Priya, and later a streaming micro-batch with a stale event.

Step 1: The seed inserts Rajesh with a million and Priya with two hundred fifty thousand, so the table starts with two rows.

Step 2: The batch merger first reduces the batch to the latest change per key using the sequence number. For Rajesh there are two updates, sequence eleven and sequence thirteen, so it keeps only sequence thirteen with the nine hundred fifty thousand balance, discarding the older one. The new account and the delete have single records each.

Step 3: The merger applies the reduced changes atomically. It inserts the new account for Amit, updates Rajesh to nine hundred fifty thousand using the latest change, and deletes Priya. After the merge the table has Rajesh updated, Priya gone, and Amit added.

Step 4: The streaming applier then processes a micro-batch of the change feed. It updates Amit to seventy-five thousand at sequence twenty and records that sequence as applied for Amit.

Step 5: The next event in the feed is an older update to Amit at sequence nineteen. The applier sees sequence nineteen is not greater than the already-applied sequence twenty, so it skips this stale event, which is how apply changes preserves correct ordering and prevents an older change from overwriting a newer one.

Step 6: The applier inserts the new account for Neha at sequence twenty-one, and the final accounts table reflects all correctly ordered changes: Rajesh at nine hundred fifty thousand, Amit at seventy-five thousand, and Neha added, with Priya deleted.

Final output:

```
Oct 30, 2026 8:52:18 AM com.bank.cdc.DeltaTable upsert
INFO: INSERT SAV2001 → Rajesh Kumar, Rs.1000000
INFO: === Batch CDC via MERGE INTO ===
INFO: MERGE reduced 4 changes to 3 latest-per-key records
INFO: INSERT SAV2002 → Amit Verma, Rs.50000
INFO: UPDATE SAV2001 → Rajesh Kumar, Rs.950000
INFO: DELETE CUR3001
INFO: After batch merge: {SAV2001=Rajesh Kumar|950000, SAV2002=Amit Verma|50000}
INFO: === Streaming CDC via APPLY CHANGES INTO ===
INFO: UPDATE SAV2002 → Amit Verma, Rs.75000
WARNING: Skipping out-of-order/stale event for SAV2002 seq=19 (already applied 20)
INFO: INSERT CUR3002 → Neha Rao, Rs.300000
INFO: Final accounts: {SAV2001=Rajesh Kumar|950000, SAV2002=Amit Verma|75000, CUR3002=Neha Rao|300000}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source DB (core banking)
    │ Debezium reads transaction log
    ▼
  Kafka change topic (op, key, values, seq)
    │ Auto Loader / Kafka source
    ▼
  Bronze CDC table
    │
    ├─ BATCH CDC ──→ reduce latest-per-key (window by seq) ──→ MERGE INTO accounts (Delta)
    │                WHEN MATCHED+DELETE → delete                (atomic upsert/delete)
    │                WHEN MATCHED → update
    │                WHEN NOT MATCHED → insert
    │
    └─ STREAMING CDC ──→ APPLY CHANGES INTO accounts
                         keys=[account_id], sequence_by=seq
                         apply_as_deletes, SCD type 1/2
                         skips stale/out-of-order events
    ▼
  accounts (Delta) stays in sync with source
  (Delta Change Data Feed can re-emit these changes to downstream layers)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Change Data Capture is about keeping a target table in sync with a source by applying only the inserts, updates, and deletes that happen in the source, rather than reloading everything. In Databricks there are two main ways to implement it. For batch or micro-batch CDC the core tool is Delta Lake's merge into, where you merge a batch of change records against the target on the primary key and, in one atomic transaction, say when matched and the operation is delete then delete, when matched then update all columns, and when not matched then insert. Because Delta is ACID, the whole merge applies atomically and concurrent readers always see a consistent snapshot. The important subtlety is that if a batch contains several changes for the same key, you must first reduce to the latest change per key using the sequence column, usually with a window function, otherwise the merge is ambiguous and you can apply an older change over a newer one.

For streaming CDC, Delta Live Tables provides apply changes into, which is purpose-built for continuous change feeds. The common pattern is to capture changes at the database with Debezium, which reads the transaction log and publishes change events to Kafka, bring them into a bronze table with Auto Loader or a Kafka source, and then apply changes into a target, specifying the key columns, the sequence column that defines ordering, and a delete condition. It handles the upsert and delete logic, deduplicates, and applies only the latest change per key even when events arrive out of order, and it can produce slowly changing dimension type one that overwrites or type two that keeps history. That removes the hand-written merge, deduplication, and ordering code you would otherwise maintain. I also keep in mind Delta's Change Data Feed, which lets a Delta table emit its own row-level changes so it can be both a CDC target and a CDC source for further layers, and the overarching rule that CDC is only correct if changes are applied in the right order per key and idempotently so a replay after failure does not corrupt the target.

At the National Bank of India our core banking database was the authoritative source for accounts, and the analytics lakehouse needed a current copy without reloading the whole table every hour. For the scheduled batches of captured changes we used merge into on the Delta accounts table, keyed on account id, reducing to the latest change per key first so that when a batch had an address update and a balance update for the same account, the newer one won. For the continuous feed from Debezium through Kafka we used apply changes into in a Delta Live Tables pipeline, which kept the accounts table in sync in near real time, skipped stale out-of-order events using the sequence, and handled deletes for closed accounts. Relying on Delta's ACID guarantees meant a mid-stream failure left the target consistent and safe to replay. So my answer is merge into for batch CDC, apply changes into for streaming CDC, always ordered by a sequence per key and backed by Delta's atomicity.
